I hit the brakes to take a picture, but didn’t even get the tip of its amazing, long tail… It was only my third Western Gray Squirrel sighting, ever. Western Gray Squirrel (Sciurus griseus) Fast moving, gray tree squirrel with a big bushy tail. These squirrels are shy, and will generally run up a tree and give a hoarse chirping call when disturbed.

It is the largest native tree squirrel in the western coastal United States. Western gray squirrels exhibit a form of coloration known as counter shading. The dorsal fur is a silver gunmetal gray, with pure white on the underside; there may be black flecks in the tail. Ears are large but without tufts. The ears turn reddish-brown at the back in the winter. The tail is long and typically very bushy.

Behavior and diet: Western gray squirrels are forest dwellers, and can be found at elevations up to 2,000 m. Time on the ground is spent foraging, but they prefer to travel distances from tree to tree. They are strictly diurnal, and feed mainly on seeds and nuts, particularly pine seeds and acorns, though they will also take berries, fungus and insects. Pine nuts and acorns are considered critical foods because they are very high in oil and moderately high in carbohydrates, which help increase the development of body fat. They feed mostly in trees and on the ground. They generally forage in the morning and late afternoon for acorns, pine nuts, new tree buds, and fruits.

Western Gray Squirrel (Sciurus griseus) Fast moving, gray tree squirrel with a big bushy tail. These squirrels are shy, and will generally run up a tree and give a hoarse chirping call when disturbed.

It is the largest native tree squirrel in the western coastal United States. Western gray squirrels exhibit a form of coloration known as counter shading. The dorsal fur is a silver gunmetal gray, with pure white on the underside; there may be black flecks in the tail. Ears are large but without tufts. The ears turn reddish-brown at the back in the winter. The tail is long and typically very bushy.

Behavior and diet: Western gray squirrels are forest dwellers, and can be found at elevations up to 2,000 m. Time on the ground is spent foraging, but they prefer to travel distances from tree to tree. They are strictly diurnal, and feed mainly on seeds and nuts, particularly pine seeds and acorns, though they will also take berries, fungus and insects. Pine nuts and acorns are considered critical foods because they are very high in oil and moderately high in carbohydrates, which help increase the development of body fat. They feed mostly in trees and on the ground. They generally forage in the morning and late afternoon for acorns, pine nuts, new tree buds, and fruits.

Western Gray Squirrel (Sciurus griseus) Fast moving, gray tree squirrel with a big bushy tail. These squirrels are shy, and will generally run up a tree and give a hoarse chirping call when disturbed.

It is the largest native tree squirrel in the western coastal United States. Western gray squirrels exhibit a form of coloration known as counter shading. The dorsal fur is a silver gunmetal gray, with pure white on the underside; there may be black flecks in the tail. Ears are large but without tufts. The ears turn reddish-brown at the back in the winter. The tail is long and typically very bushy.

Behavior and diet: Western gray squirrels are forest dwellers. Time on the ground is spent foraging, but they prefer to travel distances from tree to tree. They are strictly diurnal, and feed mainly on seeds and nuts, particularly pine seeds and acorns, though they will also take berries, fungus and insects. Pine nuts and acorns are considered critical foods because they are very high in oil and moderately high in carbohydrates, which help increase the development of body fat. They feed mostly in trees and on the ground. They generally forage in the morning and late afternoon for acorns, pine nuts, new tree buds, and fruits.
In Monterey, their most important food is underground fungi, like Rhizopogon, then fruits of California Bay, pine nuts and acorns.

description:
Three or four Tree Squirrels were chasing each other up and down and around the tree trunk. 

Western Gray Squirrel (Sciurus griseus) Fast moving, gray tree squirrel with a big bushy tail. These squirrels are shy, and will generally run up a tree and give a hoarse chirping call when disturbed.

It is the largest native tree squirrel in the western coastal United States. Western gray squirrels exhibit a form of coloration known as counter shading. The dorsal fur is a silver gunmetal gray, with pure white on the underside; there may be black flecks in the tail. Ears are large but without tufts. The ears turn reddish-brown at the back in the winter. The tail is long and typically very bushy.

Behavior and diet: Western gray squirrels are forest dwellers. Time on the ground is spent foraging, but they prefer to travel distances from tree to tree. They are strictly diurnal, and feed mainly on seeds and nuts, particularly pine seeds and acorns, though they will also take berries, fungus and insects. Pine nuts and acorns are considered critical foods because they are very high in oil and moderately high in carbohydrates, which help increase the development of body fat. They feed mostly in trees and on the ground. They generally forage in the morning and late afternoon for acorns, pine nuts, new tree buds, and fruits.
In Monterey, their most important food is underground fungi, like Rhizopogon, then fruits of California Bay, pine nuts and acorns.

https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/46023-Sciurus-griseus

My favorite Western Gray Squirrel (Sciurus griseus) observations: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=46023&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any

Western Gray Squirrel (Sciurus griseus) is a common, fast-moving, placental mammal with a big bushy tail in the Squirrels (Sciuridae) family. "These squirrels are shy, and will generally run up a tree and give a hoarse chirping call when disturbed. It is the largest native tree squirrel in the western coastal United States. Western gray squirrels exhibit a form of coloration known as counter shading. The dorsal fur is a silver gunmetal gray, with pure white on the underside; there may be black flecks in the tail. Ears are large but without tufts. The ears turn reddish-brown at the back in the winter. The tail is long and typically very bushy.
Western gray squirrels are forest dwellers. Time on the ground is spent foraging, but they prefer to travel distances from tree to tree. They are strictly diurnal, and feed mainly on seeds and nuts, particularly pine seeds and acorns, though they will also take berries, fungus and insects. Pine nuts and acorns are considered critical foods because they are very high in oil and moderately high in carbohydrates, which help increase the development of body fat. They feed mostly in trees and on the ground. They generally forage in the morning and late afternoon for acorns, pine nuts, new tree buds, and fruits." https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/46023-Sciurus-griseus

An excellent book-- (The) Monterey Pine Forest: Coastal California's Living Legacy, 2nd. ed, The Monterey Pine Forest Watch, 2018, p. 14.

Grey squirrels typically have a grayish coat, but the color can vary from silver-gray to dark gray. In some cases they may have reddish belly’s. Grey squirrels are known for their agility and are often seen leaping between trees. They are primarily herbivores, feeding on a diet of nuts, seeds, berries and occasionally insects. 

Habitats: grey squirrels are adaptable and can be found in a variety of habitats. They are commonly found in deciduous and mixed forests but can also thrive in urban and suburban areas. They build nests, called dreys, usually in the branches of trees. 

Reproduction: Breeding season from grey squirrels is typically in late winter or early spring and then again in late summer. They give birth to a litter of pups, with the number of offspring varying, but typically ranging from 2 and 5. 

Ecological impact: in regions where they have introduced, such as the United Kingdom, grey squirrels can outcompete native red squirrels, leading to declines in red populations. 

Juvenile vs. adults: juvenile squirrels are smaller than adults. They are typically about half the size of an adult squirrel. The young squirrels are more fluffy with softer fur compared to the sleeker coat of adults. Adult squirrels are larger and more robust than juveniles. The fur of adults is sleeker and more well groomed than the juveniles. Adult squirrels are more focused on foraging, nest maintenance and other adult responsibilities.

description:
I *believe* this is a Western Gray because of its overall size (comparable to our biggest resident Ground Squirrels), LARGE bushy tail (equal to or longer than the length of its body), and crisp delineation between the white underbelly and silver-gray back. HOWEVER...I will point out that this individual seems to have some ruddy coloration around its head. It is not unusual for animals in this area to take on a reddish/brownish hue around the face and forelimbs because of staining from the clay soil, which may be the case in this instance, but I wanted to point it out because it is often used to distinguish Western and Eastern Grays from one another. Ignoring coloration and only looking at structure, I would call this a Western, but bringing color into it, I am less sure.

This is a rural area with mixed farmland, forests, and meadows. I have seen both Eastern and Western Grays nearby (and occasionally in our yard, though Ground Squirrels and Chipmunks are more prevalent) with about the same frequency.
